reading.body:
Legal AI has moved from experimentation to deployment, but the profession's defining lesson is that unverified citations invite sanctions, so verification is now the industry standard.

The six reference points span guidance, cataloguing, benchmarking, purchasing data, and academic research. The ABA sets ethics guidance, Legaltech Hub maps the tools, Vals AI benchmarks legal reasoning, ILTA records what firms actually buy, and Stanford CodeX studies the underlying informatics. Together they cover what exists, what works, and what gets deployed.

This matters for AI because legal work is high-stakes text reasoning where errors carry professional liability. Independent benchmarks and ethics opinions act as gatekeepers, not raw model capability. The data does not cover compute, power, or infrastructure costs, and it gives no adoption numbers or performance scores, so it cannot support claims about scaling constraints.

summary: Research, review, and drafting assistance are deployed at scale; sanctions for unverified citations made verification the industry lesson.

analysis.body:
The clearest measured number for legal comes from the Census Bureau, and it is not legal-specific. In the Professional, scientific, and technical services sector, NAICS 54, which includes legal, 43.9% of firms answered yes to whether the business had used AI in the last two weeks, against 43.3% in the prior period. The question was first asked in September 2023. Because the figure covers the whole sector, it is context rather than a reading on law firms alone, and the sources here do not break legal out.

What firms actually deploy shows up in the vendor record. Legaltech Hub, which describes itself as a global directory where buyers research legal technology, vendors showcase solutions, and investors understand the marketplace, reports a run of moves from Relativity: the rebrand of RelativityOne to Relativity aiR in September, the launch of Relativity claiR in August, the acquisition of document automation company Gavel in June, and an MCP Connector to Claude or Legal in May. NetDocuments is building its AI strategy around a Legal Context Graph launched in May, arguing that as models and legal tools become more interchangeable, the advantage shifts to firms that connect AI to their own documents, knowledge, and legal authorities. OpenAI released Astra for Law, built initially for Am Law 200 firms and described not as a new model but as a configuration pairing GPT-6 Astra with legal-specific knowledge, tools, and ecosystem plugins. Steno's Transcript Genius mines deposition and trial transcripts for summaries, data points, and strategic insights. MiAI Law, an Australian platform, combines case law research, legislative research, case summarization, contract review, and document and pleading verification.

The pattern is research, review, drafting, and transcript work, and the money is following the same lines. ILTA, which describes itself as the trusted global resource community for legal technologists, says AI has matured rapidly since the early days of LLMs and that its Spring Peer to Peer topics reflect that evolution, and it carries Epiq's announcement of Model Context Protocol connectors for Epiq AI, Epiq Discover, Epiq Narrate, and Epiq Access. This site's own Legal Models page tracks the 1000 most-downloaded open legal models on the Hugging Face Hub, with licence, downloads, and release date, refreshed daily from the Hub's public API, alongside a lawsuit tracker, state AI laws, and compliance frameworks.

Independent testing is thinner than the vendor noise. Vals AI runs independent evaluations and benchmarks on real-world tasks, and legal research appears among them; in its reporting, one model was slowest on routine knowledge work such as MedCode, Legal Research and Public Benefits Bench. Vals also publishes cost per test and token pricing, which is the closest thing in these sources to a cost signal. None of the cited pages reports a measured return on investment for legal AI, so a buyer should treat ROI claims as uncorroborated here.

The profession's guidance sits with the American Bar Association. Its Task Force on Law and Artificial Intelligence has concluded its work, having focused on six issues including AI and the Profession, AI Risk Management, AI and Access to Justice, AI Governance, generative AI challenges, and AI and Legal Education. The ABA Center for Innovation says it will continue to address AI's impact on the profession, provide guidance on trustworthy and responsible development and use, and identify strategies to mitigate AI-related risks, and its Formal Opinion 512 on generative AI ethics is the profession's reference point. Stanford CodeX, a partnership between the law school and the computer science department, frames its work around computational models of legal systems and convenes legal experts, policymakers, and business leaders on ethical and responsible legal systems, with FutureLaw 2026 ahead.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material points to a sequence rather than a verdict. Start with the American Bar Association's guidance and Formal Opinion 512, because ethical and professional responsibility questions are the ones the profession has addressed most directly. Use Legaltech Hub to map vendors and this site's Legal Models page to see what open models exist. Use Vals AI to test whether a system reasons over legal material rather than merely sounding fluent. Treat the Census Bureau's 43.9% as sector context, not a legal adoption rate, and treat vendor announcements as announcements.

https://www.iltanet.org/.brief: ILTA, which calls itself a trusted global resource community for legal technologists, observes that AI has matured rapidly since the early days of LLMs and that its Spring Peer to Peer topics reflect this evolution. Epiq announced the availability of Model Context Protocol connectors for Epiq AI, Epiq Discover, Epiq Narrate, and Epiq Access. Litify says its ACE product now offers firm-wide AI reasoning, workflow automation, multi-step agents, and cross-platform connectivity for legal teams.

https://www.legaltechnologyhub.com/.brief: Legaltech Hub describes itself as a global directory of legal technology solutions, tools, and services where buyers can research products, vendors can showcase offerings, and investors can understand the marketplace. The page highlights that NetDocuments is building its AI strategy around a Legal Context Graph launched in May, with a new benchmark and two AI features, and that OpenAI has released Astra for Law, a configuration of its GPT-6 Astra model tailored for Am Law 200 firms with legal-specific knowledge, tools, and plugins. It also covers Steno’s Transcript Genius, which uses AI to mine deposition and trial transcripts for summaries and strategic insights, and MiAI Law, an Australian platform combining case law research, legislative research, case summarization, contract review, and document verification. A further piece examines how generative AI automating document review, first drafts, and due diligence may remove the repetitive tasks through which junior lawyers traditionally developed judgment, and how firms are experimenting with simulations and redesigned workflows to rebuild those learning opportunities.

https://law.stanford.edu/codex-the-stanf.brief: CodeX is a partnership between Stanford Law School and the Department of Computer Science that studies how information technology can improve legal processes. It applies data science and artificial intelligence to build quantitative and predictive models of the law, moving beyond traditional empirical analysis. The program offers a hands-on accelerated track for interdisciplinary student teams to prototype Agentic AI and the CFAA applications at the intersection of technology and law. CodeX also hosts a hackathon that brings together AI innovators, machine learning specialists, and legal professionals to prototype future legal technology. Additionally, it organizes an international conference and FutureLaw 2026 to bring together leaders in law, technology, and policy to discuss sustainable, ethical, and responsible AI in legal systems.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/te.brief: The World of AI catalogues what it calls the 1000 most-downloaded open legal models on the Hugging Face Hub, listing each one's licence, download count and release date. It says the catalogue is rebuilt daily from the Hub's public API, sorted by all-time downloads, with every model linking to its own Hub page. The page records its last verification date as 2026-09-28. It also advertises books and consulting services, and describes the wider site as an atlas of what the law says, who is suing whom and what the words mean, rebuilt daily from primary sources.

https://www.americanbar.org/groups/cente.brief: The Task Force on Law and Artificial Intelligence has finished its work, and the Center for Innovation will keep addressing how AI affects the legal profession, including ethical issues, trustworthy development, and risk-mitigation strategies. It will also provide guidance on responsible AI use. Past webinars from the Task Force examine how AI is reshaping law practice, covering practical applications, new legal technology, and the ethical, professional-responsibility, and regulatory challenges lawyers must navigate.
